title: The Design-Code Roundtrip That Isn't — Jonathan Gordon, ReWeaver AI
talk_summary: Jonathan Gordon argues the design↔code roundtrip is not actually solved: AI-generated code drifts from design intent and from its own prior output, and drift compounds over time like tech debt. He proposes deterministic guardrails (a fixed set of quality dimensions scanned on both code and design) wrapped around the non-deterministic LLM, with humans in control and fixes applied in a closed loop before merge.

takeaways.technique: Deterministic guardrail dimensions around LLM output
takeaways.what_they_do: Runs a fixed, deterministic set of checks across named quality dimensions (design consistency, accessibility, code quality, performance, AI-code governance) on generated code, surfacing concrete issues with an accept/refuse fix action, rather than relying on the LLM to self-review.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you do that with deterministic guardrails around the AI. The AI is still there.
takeaways.numbers: 12 iterations; pure-LLM run started at ~30% quality/fidelity; guardrails raised it, capped below 100% by ~10% human judgment

takeaways.what_they_do: Treats divergence between intended spec/design and accumulated AI-written code as a measurable, monotonically growing quantity ('drift over time is the new tech debt') and scans for it explicitly rather than assuming each PR is locally correct.
takeaways.evidence_quote: drift over time is the new tech debt and it's going to pile itself gloriously over your codebase

takeaways.what_they_do: Ran a controlled A/B: 12 iterations of pure-LLM generation vs. the same with deterministic guardrails, scoring fidelity each time, to quantify whether the guardrails actually help.
takeaways.evidence_quote: I ran another experiment, 12 iterations on a codebase with complex enough UI to it.
takeaways.numbers: 12 iterations; baseline ~30% quality; guardrailed run improved but capped by ~10% human judgment

takeaways.what_they_do: The tool never silently rewrites code: it proposes a fix, the human (or orchestrator) accepts, refuses, or undoes, keeping provenance of what changed and why.
takeaways.evidence_quote: accept or refuse. So if they know there's a fix, they will fix it. If they don't know there's a fix, they will tell you there's an issue

takeaways.technique: Local/deterministic checks to avoid token spend
takeaways.what_they_do: Puts the cheap deterministic scanning layer first and keeps the LLM optional/pluggable, claiming zero extra token cost for the core guardrail pass.
takeaways.evidence_quote: And with Ruby Weaver, there's zero extra token costs. So, we're fully local LLM
